463.title: Bigger barns (Luke 12:13–21)
463.hook: a rich man plans his retirement and dies that night
463.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich fool at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: private property is real, but its use is meant to serve the common good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman blessed his mother, and he blessed everyone who keeps the word. Your line was hear and keep it.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: Master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. It's the tone of siblings across a lawyer's table after a funeral. Jesus won't be the judge. Who made me a divider over you? He turns to the crowd: beware of all covetousness, because a man's life does not consist in the abundance of things he possesses. Then he tells a story about a farmer whose year went very, very well.
screen: `TELL MY BROTHER TO SPLIT IT.` → `WHO MADE ME A DIVIDER?` → `A FARMER'S VERY GOOD YEAR.`

segments.voice: A rich man's land brings in a huge harvest, and he has nowhere to put it all. So he talks to himself, and Luke lets us listen. What shall I do? I know. I will pull down my barns and build greater, and store everything there. And I'll say to my soul: soul, you have plenty laid up for many years, take your rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself. Notice who he's talking to. My crops, my barns, my goods, my soul. Nobody else is in the room: not his workers, not his neighbors, not the hungry, not God. Then God speaks into the room: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" He planned a retirement and didn't get an evening. And the question cuts back to the brothers at the start: whose will it all be? Jesus finishes: so is he that lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. He isn't a fool for having a good harvest or for planning ahead. Joseph stored grain in Egypt and saved lives. He's a fool because the harvest only ever went into barns. Saint Basil the Great, preaching on this parable, put it bluntly: the extra bread you store belongs to the hungry, and the shoes rotting in your closet belong to someone barefoot. The Catechism calls this the universal destination of goods: what we own is meant, in the end, to serve everyone.

464.title: Consider the lilies (Luke 12:22–34)
464.hook: the ravens don't sow, the lilies don't spin
464.howItsDone: Catholics hear this teaching on anxiety in the Gospel readings at Mass, and some pray with it when they speak of trusting God's providence, his care for all he has made.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer built bigger barns and didn't get one evening to enjoy them. Your line was this night.

Two in the morning, and the ceiling has become very interesting. Rent, a test result, a child who hasn't texted back, the thing said at work that can't be unsaid. Worry doesn't keep office hours. Right after the rich man and his barns, Jesus turns to his disciples, people who have no barns at all, and talks about exactly this. He doesn't give them a budget. He tells them to look at two things: a bird and a flower.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `WORRY KEEPS NO OFFICE HOURS.` → `A BIRD AND A FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Jesus says: be not solicitous for your life, what you'll eat, or for your body, what you'll wear. Solicitous is the Douay's word for anxious. The first picture: "Consider the ravens, for they sow not, neither do they reap, neither have they storehouse nor barn, and God feedeth them." No barn: a pointed word after yesterday. Luke says ravens, where Matthew says the birds of the air. The raven was a noisy black scavenger, and the Law of Moses listed it among the birds not to be eaten. God feeds it anyway. The second picture: "Consider the lilies, how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin." Spinning thread was daily work, the way people made cloth. The lilies make nothing, yet Solomon in all his glory wasn't dressed like one of them. Which flower did Jesus mean? Nobody knows for sure; readers have guessed anemones, irises and others. Then: which of you, by taking thought, can add to his stature one cubit? Worry adds nothing. And a tender line: fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you a kingdom. So sell what you have, give alms, make purses that don't wear out, because where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Consider means look closely, take your time. Jesus doesn't argue people out of worry. He asks them to look at something alive and let it teach them.

465.title: One more year (Luke 13:6–9)
465.hook: a fruitless fig tree gets another year of digging and dung
465.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the fig tree at Mass during Lent in the year of Luke's Gospel, a season the Church treats as a time of repentance and of God's patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ravens with no barns and lilies that never spin. Your line was fear not, little flock.

A tomato plant that never sets fruit. A rosebush that just sits there, green and stubborn, year after year. At some point you stand over it with the shovel and decide: that's it, it's coming out, and something useful is going in. Jesus tells a story about exactly that moment: an owner, a fig tree, and a gardener who asks for one thing before the shovel comes down. It's four verses long.
screen: `THE PLANT THAT NEVER FRUITS.` → `STANDING THERE WITH THE SHOVEL.` → `A GARDENER ASKS FOR ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The setting matters. Just before this, people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate while offering sacrifice, and he mentions eighteen people crushed when a tower fell at Siloam. Were they worse sinners than everyone else? No, he says, but unless you repent, you'll all likewise perish. It's a warning. Then the parable. A man has a fig tree planted in his vineyard. For three years he's come looking for figs and found none. Cut it down, he tells the dresser of the vineyard. Why should it take up the ground? The dresser answers: "Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig about it, and dung it." If it bears fruit, good. If not, then cut it down. And there the story stops. Luke never tells us what happened to the tree; the listener is left standing in the open door. Look at what the gardener does. He doesn't just ask for time. He promises work: digging around the roots so water can reach them, and spreading manure, the least glamorous job in any garden. Mercy here isn't looking the other way. It's getting your hands dirty for something that hasn't earned it. Some Christian readers, Catholic preachers among them, hear the owner as the Father and the gardener as Christ, who pleads for more time and does the digging himself. Others hear it more simply: God is patient, and patience has a deadline. Both keep the warning and the mercy together: the tree still needs to bear fruit, but it gets another year, and somebody to tend it.

Then picture the gardener's choice instead: one more year, and some digging around the roots, a conversation, a little help, a little less judgment. If you pray, pray for them.

466.title: The bent woman (Luke 13:10–17)
466.hook: eighteen years bent over, healed on the sabbath, and she stands straight
466.howItsDone: Catholics pray for the sick at Mass and through the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, in which the priest lays hands on the sick person, as Jesus did here.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gardener begged one more year for a fig tree with no figs. Your line was let it alone this year.

Try this for a moment. Let your head drop and your back curl until you're looking at the floor. Stay there. You can see feet, and dust, and the hems of other people's clothes. You can't see a face unless someone bends down to you. Now imagine that for eighteen years: going to the market like that, going to the synagogue like that. Luke says there was a woman who lived this way, and one sabbath Jesus was teaching in her synagogue.
screen: `LOOK AT THE FLOOR. STAY THERE.` → `EIGHTEEN YEARS OF FEET AND DUST.` → `ONE SABBATH IN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Luke describes her carefully: "there was a woman, who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years: and she was bent down, neither could she look upwards at all." She doesn't ask for anything. Luke only says she was there. Jesus sees her and calls her over: "Woman, thou art delivered from thy infirmity." He lays his hands on her, and immediately she's made straight, and she glorifies God. Then a complication. The ruler of the synagogue is indignant, because it's the sabbath. There are six days for work, he tells the crowd. Come and be healed on those. It's fair to see what he's protecting. Keeping the sabbath holy was, and is, a deep act of faithfulness for Jews. Jesus answers from inside that same faithfulness. Every one of you unties his ox or his donkey on the sabbath and leads it to water. And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound these eighteen years, shouldn't she be untied on the sabbath day? Daughter of Abraham: the title gives her back her full place among God's people. In Jesus' reading, the sabbath is exactly the day for setting someone free. Luke ends with the crowd rejoicing at all the glorious things he was doing.

467.title: The hen and her chicks (Luke 13:31–35)
467.hook: Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen gathers her brood
467.howItsDone: Catholics pray for their cities in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and many parishes hold processions or vigils through their neighborhoods; Psalm 91, with its shelter under God's wings, is prayed at Night Prayer on Sundays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman bent for eighteen years was made straight on the sabbath. Your line was she stood up.

When a hawk's shadow crosses the yard, a mother hen moves fast. She calls with a sharp cluck, the chicks run to her, and she spreads her wings and crouches so they disappear underneath. All you see is one puffed-up bird, staring the danger down. Whatever comes now comes to her first. Jesus is on his long road to Jerusalem when some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him. His answer starts with a fox and ends with a hen.
screen: `A HAWK'S SHADOW ON THE YARD.` → `THE CHICKS VANISH UNDER HER.` → `A FOX, THEN A HEN.`

segments.voice: First, notice who warns him. Some Pharisees come and say: get out of here, Herod wants to kill you. Not every Pharisee in the Gospels is an opponent, and these seem to be trying to protect him. Jesus answers: go and tell that fox, today and tomorrow I cast out devils and heal, and on the third day I'm finished. He won't be rushed by a fox. Then his voice turns, and he speaks to a city that isn't there. "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, that killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent to thee, how often would I have gathered thy children as the bird doth her brood under her wings, and thou wouldest not?" The Douay says bird. The Greek word can mean any bird, but it was the usual word for a hen, and English Bibles have long said hen. Not a lion or an eagle, which kings liked. A barnyard mother with nothing to fight with but her own body. Herod is the fox, and Jesus pictures himself as the hen who stands between the fox and the chicks. The Psalms already spoke this way about God, asking to be hidden under the shadow of your wings. And notice: and thou wouldest not. A hen can call; she can't make a chick run. There's grief in this line, not anger. Catholic writers have long loved the image. Saint Anselm wrote a prayer calling Jesus our mother, who gathers us under his wings like a hen.

A wedding reception, and a seating chart on an easel by the door. Table one, near the couple: family and the best friends. Table twelve, by the kitchen door: the coworkers and the plus-ones nobody's met. And at least one guest quietly moves a place card. Jesus is at a sabbath dinner in the house of a leading Pharisee, watching the guests do exactly this: angling for the first seats. So he gives them some advice.
screen: `A SEATING CHART BY THE DOOR.` → `TABLE TWELVE, BY THE KITCHEN.` → `GUESTS ANGLING FOR THE BEST SEATS.`

segments.voice: First, to the guests. Don't grab the top seat, he says. Someone more honored may arrive, the host will ask you to move, and you'll walk the whole room to the bottom in front of everybody. "But when thou art invited, go, sit down in the lowest place." Then the host may say: friend, go up higher, and you'll be honored before the whole table. It sounds like good manners, and it is. The Book of Proverbs gives almost the same advice about standing before a king. But Jesus ends with a line that goes past manners: "every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted." Then he turns to the host. When you give a dinner, don't invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives or your rich neighbors, because they'll invite you back, and that's your repayment. Instead: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind; And thou shalt be blessed, because they have not wherewith to make thee recompense." That's the harder half. You invite me, I invite you, and the account is settled. Jesus says: break the loop. Invite the people who can't pay you back, and let God do the repaying, at the resurrection of the just. The two halves fit. As a guest, don't measure your worth by your seat. As a host, don't measure your guests by what they can give. The lowest place isn't a trick for getting promoted. It's a way of sitting at a table where nobody is keeping score.

469.title: The great supper (Luke 14:15–24)
469.hook: the invited make excuses, and the poor, lame and blind are brought in
469.howItsDone: At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest invites the people with words drawn from the Book of Revelation about those called to the supper of the Lamb; some Catholic readers hear the great supper in that invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seating chart, and the last place at the table. Your line was invite the ones who can't repay.

You've planned a party. Everyone said yes, and you've cooked all day. Then, an hour before, the texts start. So sorry, something came up. Rain check? Then another. Then another. You're standing in a kitchen full of food with an empty room. At the same dinner as yesterday, a guest says something pious: blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. And Jesus answers with a story about exactly that kitchen.
screen: `THE TEXTS START AN HOUR BEFORE.` → `A KITCHEN FULL OF FOOD.` → `AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: A man makes a great supper and invites many. When it's ready, his servant goes out: come, all is ready. And they all, Luke says, begin to make excuse. I've bought a farm and I need to go see it. I've bought five yoke of oxen, and I'm going to try them out. I've married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. Some readers notice how thin these sound: who buys a farm before seeing it, or oxen before trying them? The host is angry, but he doesn't cancel. He sends the servant into the streets and lanes of the city: bring in the poor, the maimed, the blind and the lame, exactly yesterday's guests. The servant comes back: done, and there's still room. So the master says: "Go out into the highways and hedges; and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." That line has a hard history. Centuries later, compel was read as permission to force people into the faith. Saint Augustine, in a bitter fight with the Donatists in North Africa, used this verse to defend pressure from the state. The Church today reads it differently: the Second Vatican Council taught that no one may be forced to embrace the faith against their will. Read inside the story, compel sounds like the host's urgency, not violence: the servant goes out to people on the roadsides who would hardly expect an invitation, and has to insist. And at Mass, just before Communion, the priest holds up the host and says that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed, words drawn from the Book of Revelation.

segments.voice: Think of an invitation you've been dodging: a friend's dinner, a parish event, a call from your mother. Notice the excuse you've been using, and ask whether it's a farm you have to see, or something real. If you pray, thank God for the invitations in your life.
Compel. The host's command to fill his house with the poor and the people on the roads, after the invited guests skipped his feast with thin excuses. Today's word.
